title: The Leader's Guide to Giving (and Receiving) Authentic Praise
author: Jim Salvucci
summary: Salvucci builds a practical theory of workplace praise out of a small personal episode: as a bipartisan poll worker — one of the rare contexts in which the self-employed coach is actually an employee — he was unexpectedly commended by two election commissioners, and the recognition measurably increased his motivation to do tedious work well. From that he argues that praise is a genuine performance lever that most bosses squander, recalling employers who lauded 'the team' but never individuals or complimented people only transactionally to extract something. He first treats the receiving side, describing his own history as a 'praise deflector' who dismissed compliments to 'stay humble,' and reframing the graceful acceptance of praise as itself a doorway to gratitude. He then lays out seven conditions for praise that lands: it must be sincere, genuinely earned, regular but not perfunctory, delivered how the recipient can hear it, calibrated to context, timely, and from a credible source. The through-line is that heartfelt praise is a form of gratitude that benefits the giver as much as the receiver, and that mastering both giving and accepting it is a distinguishing skill of leaders rather than mere bosses.
points: Salvucci grounds praise as a motivation mechanism, not a nicety: sincere recognition from his election supervisors made him want to work harder at grueling work, and the effect persisted — evidence that authentic appreciation is a lever ordinary bosses leave unused.

He treats receiving praise as a trainable skill: as a self-described 'praise deflector' who once dismissed compliments to 'stay humble,' he argues that learning to accept recognition graciously is what unlocks gratitude and its rewards.

The essay's core is a seven-part test for praise that actually lands — sincere, genuinely praiseworthy, regular but not too regular, delivered so the person can hear it, calibrated to context, timely, and from a credible source.

He warns that inauthentic or transactional praise is worse than none at all because it is confusing, manipulative, and demoralizing, and that recognition for obvious mediocrity insults rather than motivates.

The reframe that praise is itself a form of gratitude lets Salvucci argue it rewards the giver as much as the recipient, making 'well-regulated self-praise' and the habit of noticing good work part of the leadership toolkit.
quotes: By making an effort to show sincere appreciation for my work, these commissioners inspired me to work harder.
The thing about compliments is that context matters, as do tone and word choice. You can pay a lot of compliments, but if they’re perfunctory, people will come to resent them.
Inauthentic or transactional praise is worse than none at all. It’s confusing, manipulative, and demoralizing.
Sparse praise undermines confidence. Too frequent praise can seem perfunctory.
Don’t hold your compliments till the annual review or some awards ceremony. People thrive on prompt feedback, both praise and critique.
Heartfelt praise is a form of gratitude, which means it can have a profound effect on the leader who offers it as well as on the recipient.
